paper_title: ReaDy: Recurrent States as Dynamic Context for Speculative Drafting in Hybrid Linear Attention Large Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting multiple tokens per step, yet feature-based drafters rely on target hidden features whose contextual emphasis may not align with the needs of subsequent draft positions. Hybrid linear attention (HLA) models maintain compact recurrent states that accumulate historical associations, offering an efficient source of complementary context for speculative drafting. We introduce ReaDy, the first speculative decoding method, to the best of our knowledge, to leverage HLA recurrent states for position-specific context retrieval during drafting. ReaDy equips each draft position with a learned query to retrieve supplementary context directly from the target's committed recurrent states. A lightweight state reader integrates this context into draft representations through residual updates, while low-rank state reads and fused operators keep additional computation and I/O overhead low. Building on DSpark's parallel backbone and sequential prediction head, ReaDy employs a lightweight two-stage adaptation strategy, with reader capacity, state sources, and residual placement examined through ablation studies. Across seven benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, and dialogue, ReaDy achieves an average $3.16\times$ decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding with Qwen3.8-27B on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU. It outperforms DSpark on every benchmark, improving throughput by 7.97% and acceptance length by 8.50% on average. Our code is available at https://github.com/StartLuxLabs/ReaDy.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Hybrid linear attention (HLA) offers practical route to efficient long-context language modeling. *Bohan Sun and Zunhai Su contributed equally to this work. Ngai Wong and Chuan-Wei Kuo are co-corresponding authors. By combining recurrent layers with full or sparse attention, HLA reduces the cost of maintaining context while retaining fine-grained retrieval capabilities (Yang et al., 2025; Qwen Team, 2025). Autoregressive generation nevertheless remains sequential. Speculative decoding addresses this bottleneck: lightweight drafter proposes several tokens for the target to verify together, reducing the number of target invocations needed to generate sequence (Leviathan et al., 2023). Recent advances reduce the sequential cost of drafting itself. DFlash predicts token blocks in parallel from target hidden features (Chen et al., 2026); DSpark combines parallel backbone with lightweight sequential head to capture dependencies within each block (Cheng et al., 2026). Training that exposes drafters to their own predictions or accounts for verification further improves drafttarget agreement (Li et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2026). For semi-autoregressive drafting, however, the backbone must prepare representations for several future positions at once. Its predictions therefore depend on whether the supplied context supports the needs of the entire block. Target hidden features provide selective view of the prefix. Learned under next-token prediction, they reflect context selected by the targets queries at observed positions (Liu et al., 2026). Later draft positions can require relationships that those readouts do not emphasize. The drafter can attend over the supplied features, but this does not give it direct access to the underlying target memory. KVShot enables fresh retrieval through the targets KV cache (Liu et al., 2026). That access, however, reads token-wise memory whose size grows with the prefix, increasing the I/O cost of supplying additional context. HLA offers different source: recurrent states that compactly accumulate historical associations in fixed-size matrices. Direct access to these states lets each draft position seek supplementary context Figure 1: Decoding speedups of Qwen3.8-27B on single NVIDIA B200 GPU at temperature zero. Each benchmark is normalized to autoregressive decoding. The Average panel reports the arithmetic mean of perbenchmark speedups. ReaDy improves throughput over DSpark across all seven benchmarks. with its learned query, without scanning growing token-wise cache. The challenge is to make this information useful for block prediction while keeping computation and I/O cost low. We introduce ReaDy, state-conditioned speculative decoding method for HLA models. ReaDy augments DSparks parallel backbone with reader that forms query from each draft representation, reads selected target states, and injects the retrieved context through residual update. It retains DSparks sequential prediction head and target verification, allowing only committed states to inform subsequent drafting rounds. We summarize our contributions as follows: To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to propose leveraging HLA recurrent states as complementary source of context for speculative drafting. Our theoretical analysis characterizes when new state queries can reveal information not determined by existing readouts, motivating position-specific retrieval from committed states. We develop ReaDy, recurrent-stateconditioned speculative decoding method that equips each draft position with learned state query and integrates the retrieved context through lightweight residual updates. Low-rank state reads, fused operators, and two-stage adaptation strategy enable efficient integration with pretrained drafter. Experiments across seven benchmarks with Qwen3.8-27B demonstrate that ReaDy improves decoding throughput and acceptance length over DSpark by 7.97% and 8.50% on average, respectively, achieving an average 3.16 speedup over autoregressive decoding.

sections.title: 2 Theoretical Motivation
sections.content: ReaDy builds on the distinction between recurrent state and query-specific readout of that state. We analyze this distinction at the attention-head level to motivate an additional route to prefix context. Full proofs and assumptions are given in Appendix A; Appendix reviews the underlying attention and speculative-decoding mechanisms. Query-dependent context. Target queries are learned under next-token prediction, and their readouts reflect position-specific uses of context (Liu et al., 2026). Their contextual focus need not match the needs of later positions in draft block. To isolate the selection, consider an idealized interface exposing readouts = SQ of fixed state Rdvdk , with known queries = [q1, . . . , qm]. Let ΠQ = QQ project onto their span, where is the MoorePenrose pseudoinverse. new query yields Sq = (SQ)Qq + S(I ΠQ)q. (1) The first term is the response to the component of within the exposed query span and is determined by the existing readouts. The second captures the response along directions outside that span. For unrestricted S, when this component of is nonzero, different states can agree on every exposed readout while producing different answers to q. Conversely, if has full row rank, its span covers the key space and no such ambiguity remains. The relevant issue is therefore which query directions the interface exposes, not the number of readouts alone. This idealized result concerns state-query readouts; it does not establish that the drafters complete multilayer features are insufficient. Figure 2: ReaDys state-conditioned drafting and verification process. (a) The drafter combines target hidden features with position-specific reads from committed recurrent states. Verification determines the accepted prefix and the states available in the next round. (b) Query projection maps each draft representation through rank-8 bottleneck to the 128-dimensional key space. The value map compresses the state values to rank eight. Positionspecific readouts are fused with state-scale information and injected through residual connection. Revisiting the committed state. Gated DeltaNet updates its state as Si = Si1Ai + Bi, where Ai transforms existing associations and Bi writes new ones, with raw attention readout oi = Siqi (Yang et al., 2025). Along fixed target-model continuation, define Pj = At+1 At+j and let Wj collect subsequent writes. Unrolling the recurrence gives St+j = StPj + Wj, ot+j = St (Pjqt+j) (cid:124) (cid:123)(cid:122) (cid:125) qeff +Wjqt+j. (2) The first term is the contribution of the committed prefix; the second collects the effects of future writes. The accumulated transitions change how prefix information contributes, but this contribution remains expressible as new query to St. The effective query depends on the continuation and is not available during drafting; the identity motivates learning useful query directions from draft representations. Reading St alone does not recover the second term, which depends on future writes. These observations motivate ReaDys contextaccess design. learned reader maps each draft representation to query of the same committed state, allowing the retrieved context to vary across the block without advancing the target state. Residual integration retains the backbones role in modeling the continuation and combining that context with hidden features. The fixed-size state supplies this information without token-wise memory scan. Section 3 places these reads within ReaDys semiautoregressive drafting and verification process.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: ReaDy is DSpark-based, state-conditioned speculative decoding method for HLA models. It combines block prediction with position-conditioned reads from the targets committed recurrent states (Figure 2). We use DSparks parallel backbone and sequential prediction head (Cheng et al., 2026), and introduce state-reading path in the final draft layer. Section 4.1 describes initialization and training. 3.1 State-Conditioned Block Drafting State interface. At committed prefix of length t, the target provides its hidden features and recurrent states from selected linear-attention layers. We write the state of head in layer ℓ as Sℓ,a Rdvdk , using the value-by-key convention of Section 2. These matrices summarize prefix associations without retaining separate entry for every token. All draft positions access the same committed states; the information retrieved from them depends on the representation at each position. 3 Figure 3: State-reader execution before and after optimization. Direct gathering and fused state preparation and feature packing reduce intermediate tensor materialization and redundant data movement. Green blocks indicate optimized operations. Position-conditioned reading. We place the reader in the final draft layer, after post-attention normalization and before the MLP. At this point, the draft representation has already incorporated context through the backbones existing attention path. Let hj Rd denote this representation at draft position j, and let be an RMS-normalized state. Suppressing layer and head indices, we express the read as zj = Wq RMSNorm(hj), qj = zj, qj dk uj = , = S, (3) Here Wq Rrd and Rrdk first form rankr query bottleneck, then expand it to the full key space. The query qj Rdk is thus restricted to learned subspace. Independently, Rdvr compresses the states value dimension, producing Rrdk and an r-dimensional readout uj. In our final configuration, dk = dv = 128 and = 8: the reader forms an 8 128 projected state while retaining the 128-dimensional key axis. Both constraints apply to the reader; the target continues to maintain its original 128 128 recurrent states. Fusion and residual injection. We collect the readouts from the selected layers and heads and concatenate them with their corresponding logRMS state scales to form fj. Normalization controls the scale of the state entries, while the appended log-RMS features retain information about their original magnitudes. bottleneck MLP maps 4 the fused features back to the draft width: hj = Wup SiLU(Wdown RMSNorm(fj)) , = hj + hj. (4) The draft MLP processes to produce the features used for base logits. DSparks sequential prediction head combines these logits with transition biases conditioned on the preceding token to generate the block. The residual combines retrieved prefix context with the backbones features, leaving continuation modeling to the drafter. Section 4.4 evaluates reader capacity, source layers, and injection placement. Drafting, verification, and commitment. Each round uses target hidden features and recurrent states associated with the committed history. The parallel backbone forms the draft representations, the reader supplies position-specific context, and the sequential head produces the candidate block. Under our greedy decoding setting, the target accepts the longest candidate prefix matching its argmax predictions. The first mismatch ends acceptance: the remaining proposals are discarded, and target-supplied correction is committed with the accepted prefix. If the whole block is accepted, the target supplies bonus token, unless generation has terminated. Subsequent rounds read only states associated with committed tokens; states from rejected continuations are not retained. This process repeats until EOS or the output limit. ReaDy changes how proposals are conditioned while retaining the existing verification rule. 3.2 Efficient State Access

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: State-access footprint. For selected layer head pairs, the readers source states contain dvdk elements, independent of prefix length t. token-wise KV memory with the same head count and key/value widths contains t(dk + dv) elements. This comparison concerns the contextsource footprint; actual memory traffic also depends on execution and reuse. The state-side projection is independent of draft position, so it can be shared across the queries in block. The projected states contain rdk elements, reducing the value width of each subsequent read from dv to r. Low rank reduces this read cost without eliminating the full-state access needed for preparation. This analysis concerns only the added context channel; the target and drafter retain their existing attention caches and computation. Avoiding redundant data movement. fixedsize context source can still incur substantial overhead if gathering and preparation materialize intermediate tensors. We optimize this path as illustrated in Figure 3. fused gather kernel writes selected committed states directly into preallocated execution buffer, eliminating an intermediate tensor and an additional copy. We fuse pointwise state preparation and readout feature packing to avoid separate passes over intermediate results. Native RMSNorm kernels further avoid redundant casts. These changes reduce the execution cost of the reader without changing which committed states it accesses. As shown in Figure 4, these optimizations reduce state-gather latency from 16.388 to 4.622 µs (71.8%) and state-reader latency from 65.519 to 47.094 µs (28.1%). These measurements quantify operator-level savings; end-to-end decoding gains are reported in Section 4.2. Figure 4: Operator latency before and after optimization. State gathering and state reading achieve latency reductions of 71.8% and 28.1%, respectively. 5 We evaluate ReaDys decoding performance and examine how its state-reading architecture balances draft acceptance against execution cost. 4.1 Training and Evaluation Setup Initialization and two-stage training. We use Qwen3.8-27B as the target and initialize ReaDys drafting backbone and prediction head from pretrained DSpark model (Cheng et al., 2026) released by RadixArk.1 We adapt the drafter on OpenPerfectBlend.2 In the first stage, we freeze the drafter and train only the state reader on 20k samples. In the second stage, we jointly train the reader and the drafters LoRA parameters (Hu et al., 2021) on 50k samples. The target model remains frozen throughout. Both stages use = LCE + 0.1 LL1, (5) combining cross-entropy with an L1 loss between draft and target probability distributions, without confidence loss. This objective and adaptation recipe differ from DSparks original training. Comparisons with the pretrained DSpark baseline therefore reflect both adaptation and state access; Table 2 additionally compares ReaDy with finetuning without state access. Appendix describes the data mixture, loss aggregation, and optimizer settings. Inference settings. We compare ReaDy with autoregressive (AR) decoding and the pretrained DSpark drafter. Each model instance runs on one NVIDIA B200 GPU with SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024), using BF16 without quantization and request concurrency of one. Evaluation requests are distributed across GPUs, with each input compared across methods on the same GPU. All methods use greedy decoding (temperature zero), with thinking enabled, maximum of 1,024 output tokens, and context limit of 16,384 tokens. Generation stops upon EOS. Both DSpark and ReaDy use draft block size of seven. The curves show cumulative survival, not acceptance conditional on earlier positions. Benchmarks and metrics. We evaluate seven benchmarks across three task categories. Mathematical reasoning is evaluated on GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) and MATH500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021). For code generation, we use sanitized MBPP (Austin et al., 2021), HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), and LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2024). Dialogue and instruction following are evaluated using the first turn of MT-Bench (Zheng et al., 2023) and fixed Alpaca subset (Taori et al., 2023). We report server-side decoding throughput in tokens per second (TPS), excluding prefill. Acceptance length is the total number of output tokens divided by the total number of verification rounds, including tokens supplied by the target model; it therefore measures the average progress per verification. For the overall throughput comparison, we first average TPS across benchmarks and then compute speedups from these averages. 4.2 Main Results Table 1 shows that ReaDy improves both throughput and acceptance length on every benchmark. Its mean decoding throughput reaches 302.78 tokens/s, compared with 95.86 for AR decoding and 280.42 for DSpark, yielding 3.16 speedup over AR and further 7.97% gain over DSpark. The improvement extends across task types: throughput gains over DSpark range from 6.43% to 8.66% on mathematics and code generation, and reach 9.45% on MT-Bench and 9.83% on Alpaca. The corresponding overall acceptance-length gain is 8.50%. Thus, the additional progress per verification is sufficient to offset the cost of state retrieval in the evaluated setting. The slightly smaller throughput gain also highlights the need to control reader overhead, which motivates the design comparisons below. Appendix illustrates how an early mismatch affects block acceptance in an individual generation. 6 Reader capacity. Table 3 compares ranks 8, 16, 32, and 128 in both key and value spaces. Increasing rank from eight to 128 raises mean acceptance length from 4.5285 to 4.5404, but reduces the throughput gain over DSpark from 7.97% to 7.81%. Rank eight retains most of the acceptance benefit and gives the highest measured throughput, supporting compact supplementary readout. Table 3: Reader rank. We therefore examine all seven proposed positions using the final checkpoint. Figure 5 reports cumulative prefix survival for Math (GSM8K), Code (HumanEval), and Chat (MT-Bench). At position j, this is the fraction of eligible drafting rounds in which all of the first proposed tokens are accepted, rather than the acceptance probability conditional on earlier positions surviving. ReaDy has higher prefix survival at every position in all three benchmarks. At the seventh position, survival increases from 45.98% to 58.17% on GSM8K, from 25.89% to 31.19% on HumanEval, and from 12.59% to 16.11% on MTBench. Thus, larger fraction of ReaDys complete seven-token proposals survive verification. Appendix describes the measurement protocol and its scope. 4.4 Ablation Studies Fine-tuning without state access. To assess the benefit beyond additional training, Table 2 includes fine-tuned DSpark variant without the state adapter. Fine-tuning alone raises throughput from 280.42 to 286.50 tokens/s and acceptance length from 4.1739 to 4.2732, confirming that adaptation contributes to the improvement over the original checkpoint. ReaDy further reaches 302.78 tokens/s and an acceptance length of 4.5285: gains of 5.68% and 5.97%, respectively, over this no-state variant. This comparison supports an additional benefit from state-conditioned adaptation. The 7.97% throughput gain over pretrained DSpark therefore reflects both continued adaptation and state access. sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented ReaDy, DSpark-based, stateconditioned speculative decoding method for HLA models. Its reader retrieves position-specific context from committed recurrent states and integrates it with draft representations through residual updates. Low-rank reads and fused operators control the additional I/O overhead. ReaDy achieves an average 3.16 speedup over autoregressive decoding and 7.97% throughput improvement over DSpark across seven benchmarks on Qwen3.8-27B using single NVIDIA B200 GPU. These results demonstrate the value of recurrent-state retrieval for improving draft agreement and decoding efficiency within DSparks semi-autoregressive architecture. Future work will explore training the complete drafter from scratch and learning to allocate state access and readout capacity across draft positions.

sections.title: References
sections.content: Target context reuse for speculative drafting. Drafters can reuse target hidden features or query target memory directly. GliDe (Du et al., 2024) and LongSpec (Yang et al., 2026) access the targets KV cache through cross-attention. KVShot (Liu et al., 2026) compares hidden-feature and KVcache reuse, highlighting the trade-off between richer context and retrieval cost. Although cache sharing avoids duplicate storage, reading tokenwise history incurs memory traffic that grows with the number of attended tokens. ReaDy instead queries fixed-size recurrent states, using low-rank reads and fused operators to limit the additional I/O cost. Speculative decoding for recurrent and hybrid models. Recurrent targets require dependencyaware verification and recovery of accepted states. Wang et al. (2024) address these challenges for Mamba and hybrid models; STree (Wu et al., 2025) extends tree verification to hybrid state-space models. SpecLA (Wang et al., 2026) combines topology-aware verification and factor-based state recovery with EAGLE-style drafting from recurrent target features. ReaDy focuses on positionconditioned reads of committed states for block drafting. sections.content: Training data. Open-PerfectBlend is public instruction mixture covering mathematics, code, conversation, and instruction following. Its eight source corpora are listed in Table 7, using counts reported by the dataset card. The card reports removing 88.1k examples during deduplication. These counts describe the public mixture, rather than the source proportions of our 20,000and 50,000sample adaptation sets. Training mode. In its offline experiments, the original DSpark paper (Cheng et al., 2026) regenerates responses to Open-PerfectBlend prompts using each target model and adopts non-thinking mode for data generation and evaluation. We first normalize within each sequence, as above, then average the sequence losses across the four training GPUs. The confidence-loss weight is zero. We use no additional KL-divergence, featurereconstruction, or reward loss. Relation to DSpark training. We reuse pretrained DSpark drafter, but do not reproduce its original training recipe. The published DSpark objective combines cross-entropy, probabilitydistribution L1, and confidence losses with weights 0.1, 0.9, and 1.0, respectively (Cheng et al., 2026). sections.title: C Qualitative Example
sections.content: Figure 6 compares seven-token proposals from DSpark and ReaDy at the same summary prefix in an Alpaca story-summarization example. DSpark first differs from the target at the third position, proposing harvested where the target produces produced. This mismatch ends its accepted prefix after two proposed tokens, even though its remaining displayed tokens match the target continuation. ReaDy matches all seven target tokens. The example illustrates how agreement at an early draft position determines how much of the proposed block can be accepted.

sections.title: D Background
sections.content: D.1 Linear and Hybrid Linear Attention During autoregressive decoding, full attention reads token-wise keys and values whose storage grows with the prefix. Kernel linear attention instead aggregates past keyvalue associations into recurrent state (Katharopoulos et al., 2020). For positive feature map ϕ, causal attention head can be written as St = St1 + vtϕ(kt), zt = zt1 + ϕ(kt), Stϕ(qt) ϕ(qt) ot = , (D.1) with zero initial states. Here qt, kt, and vt are the current query, key, and value; zt supplies the normalization. At fixed feature dimensions, the state size and the cost of one recurrent update and readout are independent of prefix length. The state stores aggregated associations, whereas the query selects particular readout. 11 Figure 6: An Alpaca story-summarization example. Green highlights accepted proposed tokens; red marks the first mismatch. DSpark matches two of the seven proposals before its first mismatch, while ReaDy matches all seven. These counts refer only to accepted draft proposals, excluding target-supplied tokens. Subsequent designs improve how this limited memory is updated. Data-dependent gates control retention, while delta-rule updates revise the association addressed by the current key. Gated DeltaNet combines these mechanisms (Yang et al., 2025). For one head with normalized keys, its update can be written as (cid:101)St = αtSt1, et = vt (cid:101)Stkt, St = (cid:101)St + βtetk , ot = Stqt. (D.2) In the original parameterization, the inputdependent gates αt, βt (0, 1) control retention and write strength, respectively. The decay gate first attenuates the previous state. The delta term then corrects the difference between the incoming value vt and the value retrieved by kt from that decayed state. This supports both global forgetting and targeted update to the current keyvalue association. Here ot denotes the raw attention readout, before the blocks output normalization and gating; the kernel-attention denominator in Equation D.1 is not used. Expanding Equation D.2 gives used in Section 2 to separate the contribution of the committed prefix from subsequent writes. Hybrid linear attention interleaves recurrent layers with full-attention layers, combining compact state-based context modeling with access to individual cached tokens (Qwen Team, 2025). The recurrent layers maintain fixed-size states, while fullattention layers retain growing KV caches. This layer organization also shapes activation dynamics: massive activations form spikes before fullattention layers and can persist as plateaus across intervening linear-attention layers (Su et al., 2026). ReaDy accesses the recurrent states as supplementary context for drafting, without changing the targets hybrid architecture. D.2 Speculative Decoding In standard speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023), an autoregressive drafter samples block of candidates y1, . . . , yb. Let qj and pj denote the draft and target distributions conditioned on the committed prefix and y<j. The target evaluates these prefixes in parallel. The original hiddenfeature path and the added recurrent-state path therefore expose different interfaces to target context. The methods have different drafting boundaries, so their curves aggregate different rounds along identical output sequences. The checkpoint has training/evaluation overlap: these measurements characterize its decoding behavior and do not establish held-out generalization. They also do not isolate semantic retrieval mechanism. where [x]+ = max(x, 0). If all candidates are accepted, an additional token is sampled from pb+1. This procedure preserves the target distribution. Our greedy evaluation accepts the longest prefix matching the targets argmax predictions. The first mismatch ends the accepted prefix. Our reported τ counts all committed tokens per verification, including target-supplied correction or bonus tokens, rather than only accepted proposals. Except when generation terminates, accepting proposals yields + 1 committed tokens. D.3 Target and Drafter Architectures Hybrid target model. Qwen3.8-27B has dense language backbone with 64 layers and hidden width 5,120.3 Its layer pattern repeats three Gated DeltaNet layers followed by one gated fullattention layer, yielding 48 recurrent layers and 16 full-attention layers. The former retain fixed-size matrix states, while the latter use token-wise KV caches. The published configuration specifies 128dimensional recurrent keys and values, giving the 128 128 per-head states accessed by ReaDy. Under zero-based indexing, the selected source layers 30 and 62 are both recurrent layers. ReaDy leaves this hybrid target architecture unchanged and adds read-only interface to its committed recurrent states. DSpark architecture. DSpark (Cheng et al., 2026) combines DFlash-based parallel backbone (Chen et al., 2026) with lightweight sequential prediction head. The backbone processes block in one forward pass to produce position-wise representations and base logits. sequential head adds transition biases conditioned on earlier proposals: the papers Markov variant uses the preceding token through low-rank transition map, while its RNN variant carries within-block hidden state. DSpark also introduces confidence-based verification scheduling, separately from this drafting architecture. ReaDy supplies additional target-state context to the backbone through residual updates. Checkpoint used in this work. The RadixArk Qwen3.8-27B-DSpark model card describes five full-attention draft layers with hidden width 5,120, 32 query heads, and eight KV heads. It receives auxiliary target features from layers 5, 19, 33, 47, and 61 and uses rank-256 Markov head.
